definition: Maelstrom means a violent whirlpool that sucks objects in — or, figuratively, a churning, overwhelming storm of events or feelings.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word maelstrom. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know maelstrom should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: One blunt sentence in a late-night interview pulled the actress into a maelstrom of criticism that churned online for weeks.
A commotion is noisy but brief — a dropped tray of dishes; a maelstrom churns violently and pulls everything nearby into itself.
A cataclysm is stronger than even a maelstrom: not just a churning storm that pulls everything in, but a disaster that levels everything at once.

A whirlpool is spinning water that pulls things toward its center, and the word mostly stays in the water. A maelstrom is the violent, monstrous version — and the one that goes figurative: careers and countries get pulled into maelstroms. Every maelstrom is a whirlpool; only the overpowering ones earn the name.

Vortex is the neutral, almost technical word for any whirling mass that sucks things inward — air, water, particles in physics. Maelstrom keeps its storm-violence even in figurative use: a maelstrom of criticism batters as it pulls. A vortex merely draws you in; a maelstrom churns you once you arrive.

Turmoil is violent confusion and agitation — a state that minds, crowds, and countries can be in. It churns, but it does not pull. A maelstrom adds the whirlpool's defining action: it drags everything nearby into itself, so bystanders and innocents end up sucked into the middle.

Maelstrom means a violent whirlpool that sucks objects in — or, figuratively, a churning, overwhelming storm of events or feelings.
In the panic of 1929, the stock market became a maelstrom that pulled down banks, brokers, and family savings alike.
Like a whirlpool, the crash did not damage just one thing — it churned violently and sucked in everything near it, which is the defining image of a maelstrom.

Maelstrom keeps the violent energy of its whirlpool origin even in figurative use — a maelstrom of criticism, a maelstrom of emotions — so save it for situations that genuinely churn and overwhelm, not for ordinary busyness.
Compare its unit cousins: a quagmire traps you and a morass confuses you, but a maelstrom batters you.

The bus drivers walked out on a Monday, asking for little more than a cost-of-living raise.
By Thursday the walkout had grown into a maelstrom that pulled in half the city.
Schools closed when teachers could not cross town; the port backed up; even the courts postponed hearings.
Shopkeepers with no stake in the dispute found their aisles empty, dragged into a fight they had never joined.
When it ended three weeks later, people remembered the churn more than the raise — how one strike had sucked everything nearby into its spin.
